AW Next is a desktop app for Windows and Linux. Releases include their own runtime, so Node.js is needed only to build from source. On Linux, install the AppImage as Linux and the Steam Deck describes, then come back: everything below applies, with ~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next in place of %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next.

Windows 10 and 11 Linux (x64, beta) --- --- --- Get it From the latest release: Achievement.Watcher.Setup.<version>.exe, or Achievement.Watcher.Portable.<version>.zip to keep its data beside the app From the same release: Achievement.Watcher.<version>.AppImage Start it Run the installer, choose a folder, then open AW Next from the Start menu chmod +x, then run it. It needs FUSE 2: libfuse2t64 on Ubuntu 24.04 Data %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next (the portable build keeps a data folder beside the executable) ~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next The installer is signed with the project's own self-signed certificate (CN=Shirow), so Windows SmartScreen may still ask for confirmation. See Antivirus or SmartScreen warning. In-app updates install only a release signed by that certificate, pinned by thumbprint.

Six steps: basics, profile, games, sources, look and alerts, and a final recap The first-run guide asks for the choices that fill the library: Basics: the language (interface, and game metadata when a source offers it) and the interface, Simple or Advanced (see below). Neither is preselected. Profile: the name shown in the header, an optional local avatar and your main Steam account. Games: what was found on this PC, with counts. Add a folder only if something is missing. Sources: optional sign-ins (Steam, Epic, Xbox, PlayStation, RetroAchievements) that read your real library and unlocks made on another PC. You can skip them and connect later in Settings → Sources. Every source switch is under Fine-tune sources, folded away because the defaults read whatever is installed. Pick one in the first-run guide, and change it any time with the Interface control at the top of Settings. The Interface control sits beside the panel title; the search field filters every tab at once Simple shows the everyday tabs: General, Appearance, Controller, Notification, Notification presets, Sources, Folders and Help. Advanced adds the Steam / GBE Fork, Ubisoft / Uplay R1/R2 and Advanced tabs, and the deeper options inside the other tabs. Simple hides controls and never turns anything off. Tracking, scanning and notifications behave the same, and every value you set is still there when you switch back. Game Health follows the same idea: Simple says Achievement data found or Detected when the game starts, Advanced gives exact counts, files and process names. An existing installation upgrades to Advanced, so nothing you used disappears. The search field at the top of Settings filt

In Settings → Sources, the shield marks the official desktop libraries. Enable a row and refresh; only libraries detected on this PC appear. See Compatible sources. The selector between the library search and the + button switches between six views: large cards, portrait covers, their two compact variants, a list, and a details table with playtime and last session. The choice is saved, and every view has the same cards, filters and context menu. The Details view: latest achievement, last session and playtime for every game at a glance Settings → Appearance → Library tiles sets the tile size and the gap between tiles (down to 0), and shows or hides the game name, progress bar, platform icon, health dot and the two buttons, for every view at once. A game Steam lists with no achievements shows its artwork instead of a bar; Bar of games without achievements brings the bar back. Right-click a

Collections are your own groups of games. Right-click a game, choose Collections, and tick one or make a new one. The collections button next to the installed-only toggle filters the library to one collection, and the profile numbers follow. Create a collection, add games from their right-click menu, then filter the library by it Viewing one collection: the button takes its icon and colour, and the totals count only its games A collection has a name, a colour and an icon or a picture of your own. Edit collection… in the button's menu opens the editor, where you also delete it; its games stay in the library. The collection editor

The round button beside the completion rate in the profile header opens Library stats: overall completion, unlocked and locked counts, the average per game, average and tracked playtime, trophy counts, and one row per platform. Show installed games only limits the totals to this PC. The arrow beside the button folds the profile header into one row, which gives the library more room (Settings → Appearance → Profile has the same choice). The overview: completion, counts, average per game and playtime Trophies counts a platinum for each finished game (a PlayStation game once its platinum trophy is earned) and grades every other unlocked achievement by rarity, with the thresholds under the bar (they follow the rarity setting in Notifications). Platinum games lists what you finished and when, Rarest achievements the hardest ones you hold, and All achievements opens the full list. Trophies, pl

Settings → Appearance paints the whole app and the in-game overlay. Thirteen palettes are built in, and every one can be edited: pick a theme and the editor opens on its colours, one row per layer (window background, top bar, library panel, cards and rows, settings window, text, muted text, borders, accent). Each layer takes a colour with an opacity and optionally a gradient, and the five surface layers can also take a background image with a fit and either a coloured veil or a blur. Editing previews live and writes nothing. Save theme makes it a theme of your own: keep the name to replace that theme, or type another to get a second one. Custom… is the scratch slot, always editable and never overwritten by a save made from it. Reset all restores the theme you are editing: a built-in returns its own palette, a saved or imported theme returns what is on disk, and Custom returns to the defa

Settings → Help is a live reference, grouped by how a question arrives: Get started, Something is wrong, Emulated games and Make it yours. It shows your real hotkey, controller layout and bindings, theme and notification mode, and refreshes as you change settings. Its search ignores case and accents, and every topic is available in both interface modes.

Open Settings → Folders and pick a path: Smart Find offers everything it finds for approval before adding anything. It recognises library folders by name ("Games", "Jeux", "Repacks" and their equivalents in twenty-odd languages, plus "Emulators" and "Emulation") on every drive, and it reads what the launchers recorded: Epic manifests, GOG Galaxy and Ubisoft Connect registry entries, and the pointer Windows writes for the drive you chose for Xbox games. That finds a library named after a storefront (D:\Epic Games, D:\XboxGames) without scanning. Games a launcher owns keep their own source. Smart Find adds everything else in the same folder, usually where a repack or a Goldberg build ends up. Add a Folder watches a location you select. Generate configs runs a fuller scan and can apply enabled emulator setup options. If a folder is rejected, select the directory that directly contains the s

Settings → Notification sets the delivery mode: Automatic (the default: the in-game overlay when it can be shown, a Windows or desktop notification when it cannot, and never the same unlock twice), In-game overlay, Windows notification, or Both. If Windows Do Not Disturb hides notifications while you play, enable Priority notifications and approve the one-time request. Test buttons let you try everything before launching a game. See Notifications and what Automatic looks at.

A game tile's tools button opens its Game Health panel: whether AW Next can see the game, read its achievements and announce its unlocks, and the repairs that apply. It is the first thing to open before reporting a problem (see Game Health). To play a game again from zero, use Reset achievements, which backs everything up first.

Closing the main window keeps AW Next in the system tray, where the background tracker keeps watching files and processes for playtime and unlocks. With no window open it hands its memory back to Windows, and the periodic library scan waits while a game runs. Settings → Advanced → Automatic achievement data updates turns that scan off for anyone who maintains steamcache by hand. Whether AW Next starts with Windows and closes to the tray is under Settings → General. To exit fully, use the tray menu.

Installed releases check the project's GitHub release feed, never during a game. A new version is announced by a desktop notification and a title-bar chip (the tray icon also shows a blue dot), and nothing takes the focus from a game or another app. The notice stays until you close it and returns after a game. Click the notification or the chip to open the update window. It shows the release notes of every version you skipped and the download size, with Update now, Later and Skip this version. Nothing downloads before you choose. After Update now, the same window follows the download, which you can cancel or send to the background. The title-bar chip shows the state and brings the window back. When the download finishes, the installer shows its own progress card and AW Next restarts. If a game is running, the install waits for it to close, or you can install anyway from the window. Setti

A source is one place AW Next reads achievements from: a launcher's local data, a Steam-compatible save file, or a console emulator's trophy file. Each source has its own switch in Settings → Sources. Each source is a separate switch; the shield marks the official desktop libraries After enabling a source, refresh the library. Only libraries detected on this PC are shown.

These read the launcher's own local data and carry a shield in Settings. Steam, Epic, Xbox PC and PlayStation can each be connected from Settings to read what the local files do not carry. Every token is encrypted before it is stored on this PC, and everything else works without any account. Account What connecting adds --- --- Steam Two switches, off by default and shown while the Steam source is Owned: add the games you own and add the games shared with you through Steam Family. They let a private profile, or one that never installed most of its library here, list the right games. Each makes the first scan noticeably longer, since every added game resolves its achievements and artwork once. A game with nothing to read locally is then read from your Steam profile, which needs its game details public; the answer is cached for six hours. AW Next reads the achievement and stats files that Steam emulators write (achievements.json, achievements.ini, achievements.bin, stats.ini and compatible layouts) from the places those tools use. That covers Goldberg and GBE Fork (which AW Next can also install and repair), GreenLuma, LumaPlay, SmartSteamEmu, CreamAPI, the Nemirtingas emulators and scene releases with a compatible layout. For a game whose files are elsewhere, add the folder under Settings → Folders. The folders AW Next checks on its own, and the ones you add - per-game saves or whole libraries A portable CODEX, RUNE or CPY release normally writes to %PUBLIC%\Documents\Steam\ \<appid>, but a portable copy keeps that tree inside the game folder, where nothing looks for it. Adding the game's own folder under Settings → Folders is enough: its steamemu.ini (or cpy.ini) names the AppID, and the save tree is looked for beside i

Emulator Console Trophy / achievement file --- --- --- RPCS3 PlayStation 3 TROPUSR.DAT beside the trophy list ShadPS4 PlayStation 4 TROP.XML, which holds the list and the earned state KytyPS5 PlayStation 5 Trophies\<title>\trophies.json beside the emulator; the list comes from the game's scesys\trophy2 package Xenia Xbox 360 .gpd, which also holds both Each is watched live, so an unlock raises a notification like any other. RPCS3, ShadPS4 and Xenia can move their data off the default path, and AW Next reads the settings the emulator reads: RPCS3: the trophy folder follows vfs.yml (including a $(EmulatorDir)-relative remap), a portable folder beside the executable, and RPCS3CONFIGDIR. ShadPS4: recognised whether you point at the emulator, its user folder, gamedata itself, or (since 0.19) its trophy folder or home\<user>\trophy. Its config is read from either place shadPS4 has kept it. Xen

Games played on any emulator that reports to RetroAchievements come from your account, not from a file. Turn on the RetroAchievements source and fill in the account card under it: your username and the Web API key from retroachievements.org/settings. The key is encrypted before it is stored on this PC. The RetroAchievements switch, with the Epic and Steam account cards under it Import library adds every game you played, with its achievements, unlock dates, points and rarity. A second import fetches only the games whose progress moved, and a game played for the first time is added on its own. New unlocks are announced within seconds while an emulator that reports to RetroAchievements runs (RetroArch, DuckStation, PCSX2, PPSSPP, Dolphin, BizHawk, Project64 or any other RA-integrated build, recognised by name or by the RetroAchievements dll beside it), and within a few minutes otherwise. Source What it is --- --- Xbox 360 games recompiled for PC ReXGlue ports and similar keep their achievement list in an achievements folder (.toml, .tsv) or SaveData\Achievements.json, in the game folder or in Documents\<game>. The list comes from the game's own default.xex, in every language it ships, with secret achievements kept secret. dbox.tools adds DLC achievements and Exophase the share of players per achievement. A list in Documents is found on its own; for one in the game folder, add that folder under Settings → Folders or use Smart find. Unlocks are notified live, playtime is tracked, and Reset achievements works. More than sixty known ports (Sonic Unleashed, Sonic the Hedgehog through Marathon Recompiled, Blue Dragon re:Blue, Lost Odyssey, Perfect Dark Zero, Fable II, Gears of War 2, Forza Motorsport 4, GoldenEye 007, Skate 2 and others) are listed from their executable before

sections.h: Steam metadata, without an API key
sections.x: AW Next uses no Steam Web API key and no connected Steam account for this. Each game's list comes from a keyless chain: the official GetGameAchievements endpoint first (hidden descriptions, icons, global rarity and Steam's achievement sets), then the SteamCommunity achievements page (the same schema, in your language), then SteamHunters, and a browser scrape only as a last resort. As on Steam, an achievement the developer archived counts only if you earned it. Otherwise it is left out of the list, the percentage and the platinum notification. Results are cached per language in %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\steamcache\schema, so local sources and games seen before work offline. Steam never announces that an update added achievements, so a cached list re-checks itself every 3 days and picks up new ones without removing any. To check at once, use Settings → Advanced → Recheck achieveme

In Simple mode the Sources list folds away six niche rows: GreenLuma, LumaPlay, the two Nemirtingas emulators (the GOG and Epic save readers), Goldberg SocialClub and the notification-cache import. A row folds only while it is enabled and no game in your library came from it. Switch one off, or own a game it detected, and the row returns, so the interface mode never hides the control that would explain a missing game. Advanced always lists every source. -- Next: Notifications, to choose how unlocks are announced. Source-specific setup: Goldberg / GBE · Uplay R2 · Game Health ← Documentation · Project home

AW Next announces an unlock with a native Windows notification (toast), an in-game overlay popup, or both. Choose how under Settings → Notification. On Linux the notification is the desktop's own (GNOME or KDE) and the overlay works the same way. Do Not Disturb and the Priority notifications switch are covered in Supported desktops. One delivery mode, one preset - Automatic handles the rest

Mode Behavior --- --- Automatic (default) The in-game overlay when it can be shown, a Windows notification when it cannot. In-game overlay Always the styled popup above the running game, even in exclusive fullscreen, where it may not be visible. If the overlay cannot display at all, that notification arrives as a Windows notification. Windows notification Always the Windows system notification. Achievement and progress notifications use the achievement icon; playtime notifications can include game artwork and a progress bar. Both The same event on both transports. AW Next posts Windows notifications itself and starts no other program, PowerShell included, so they appear at once. A custom app id set in options.ini ([notificationadvanced] appID) still goes through the former PowerShell route. The library window can stay closed in every mode: the background tracker handles delivery. The ove

Each notification is routed once, from what AW Next can observe at that moment: Situation What happens --- --- Nothing covering the screen In-game overlay. The game is in fullscreen (Direct3D with Windows' fullscreen optimizations, which most games get) Windows notification, shown over the game without taking its focus: a priority notification when those are on, otherwise a reminder that AW Next closes after the usual notification time. Borderless and windowed games keep the overlay. The game holds the screen in legacy exclusive mode (older games, many OpenGL games, or fullscreen optimizations off) Nothing from another app is drawn on that screen. The notification goes to Notification Center; its sound and the controller rumble still play. Borderless mode in the game brings it back on screen. The app cannot display the popup (no usable preset, renderer unavailable) A Windows notification

sections.h: Where the current state is shown
sections.x: A game's Game Health panel has a Notifications row naming the transport that delivered the last notification and why, for example Working - Windows fallback active (Simple mode). With no notification yet it shows the configured mode. If Windows kept a notification in Notification Center because the game was full screen or Do Not Disturb was on, the row says so. See Game Health.

Full-screen games and other automatic Windows rules can turn on Do Not Disturb, which sends ordinary toasts to Notification Center without showing them. Settings → Notification → Priority notifications marks achievement unlocks as important. Windows asks once whether AW Next may send them; change the answer in Windows notification settings. It is off by default and covers achievement and completion unlocks only, never progress or playtime. The toast uses the urgent scenario, which needs Windows 11 (build 22546) or later; on Windows 10 the setting does nothing. See Microsoft's app-notification documentation.

Steam shows its own pop-up for the games it runs, so AW Next stays quiet for them by default. Enable Settings → Notification → Steam client games to get AW Next's notification too, with its sound, overlay, rarity and screenshot souvenir. It covers owned games and games added through SteamTools, LuaTools or GreenLuma: AW Next follows the stats file Steam rewrites in appcache\stats. To keep only AW Next's notification, turn off Steam → Settings → Notifications → I unlock an achievement.

The look of the in-game popup is a preset: ten ship with the app, you can design your own, and a preset can be shared as one .awpreset file. See Presets and the Preset Designer. Opacity (30% to 100%) in the same settings sets how see-through the popup is.

Import .wav, .mp3, .ogg, .flac, .m4a or .aac files from the Notification settings. Random in the sound list plays a different file from yours for every notification, and for every preview or test. Rare achievement sound and 100% completion sound (Advanced mode) give those popups their own sound, for the overlay and Windows notifications. Both start on "Same as unlocks"; "None" makes that kind of popup silent. A sound chosen for one game in its own panel still wins. Progress sound (Advanced mode) does the same for progress popups. It wins over a game's own sound, except for a game set to no sound. To silence one game's progress popups, right-click it and mute its progress. Emulators (Advanced mode) gives each console its own preset and sound: Xenia, RPCS3, shadPS4 and Kyty are listed. Recompiled Xbox 360 games follow Xenia's choice, PS4 ports follow shadPS4's, and Same as main keeps the m

Choose a corner, edge or centered position in the Notification settings. Positions are measured against the whole screen, so a bottom anchor sits on the bottom edge, not above the taskbar, and the card touches the chosen edges whatever room for shadow or glow its preset leaves around it. AW measures each preset once per position, in the background after its first popup, so that first popup shows at the old place. A preset whose card follows the length of its text (PS5 Steam, Slim) is measured with each popup, which holds it back about half a second. Reposition moves the custom position, used exactly as you left it; one saved on a monitor that is gone is brought back into view. With several screens, the popup appears on the screen of the game you are playing, not the one under the mouse, and a custom position keeps its place relative to that screen. Windows notifications always show on th

Counter achievements (kill 50 enemies, travel 100 km) can raise a progress popup at every step. In Advanced mode, Progress position and Progress scale give those popups their own place and size. Same as unlocks, the default, follows a game's own position when it has one; any other choice applies to the progress popups of every game. The crosshair beside Progress position places a custom anchor for progress only. These settings move only the in-game popup. Progress milestones, in the common notification settings, shows a progress notification only when a counter crosses another 10, 25 or 50% of its goal. It applies to the popup and the Windows notification. The unlock itself is always shown. The overlay list has its own keyboard shortcuts (see the Overlay guide) and optional gamepad control (see the Controller guide).

Open a game's tools panel and choose Notification to give that game its own popup preset, position, sound or scale. Every field inherits the global setting, and only the values you change are stored; sound also offers silence and random. The crosshair beside Position drags a preview to where that game's popup should appear. The five test buttons preview that game and its artwork without changing achievement progress. A removed preset or sound falls back to the global value, and renaming a user preset keeps its game assignments. Right-click a game to mute its progress notifications while keeping unlocks and completion notifications. An achievement with a global unlock rate at or below the rare limit prints its percentage and gets the preset's rare styling: gold at 5% or less, silver up to 10%, bronze up to 15%. Move these limits with Settings → General → Rarity thresholds set to Custom (A

Settings → General → Rarity display switches to Trophy mode: every achievement is graded by its global unlock rate (gold under 20%, silver under 50%, bronze otherwise or when the rate is unknown) in the game window, the overlay, the profile trophies and the notification. Rarity thresholds moves the bounds. All three grades use the preset's rare styling (state-rare plus tier-gold, tier-silver or tier-bronze); platinum stays the separate completion state. The app gives a preset its tier in rarityTier (with rarityMode and the localized rarityGrade); a preset without the field falls back to the percentage. With a PlayStation account connected (Settings → Sources), a game that also came out on PlayStation uses its real trophy list, wherever its achievements come from: each achievement takes the grade and DLC group of the trophy with the same name or description. The real platinum shows in eve

Capturing the popup as a window does not work: the popup window lives a few seconds, so OBS never catches it. Use a Browser source, which OBS keeps loaded for the whole stream. Settings -> Notification -> OBS browser source. Preview opens the page in your browser with a sample unlock every ten seconds, the quickest check that the chain works. Copy link copies the address. In OBS: + -> Browser, paste the address into URL. Set any Width and Height. The card scales to fill the box. The source shows the same preset, artwork and rarity styling as the in-game popup and follows the preset you pick in Settings. The test buttons under Settings -> Notification fire into it too, whatever the delivery mode. A bigger source is a sharper card. The card is laid out at the source's size, not stretched. Give the source roughly twice the preset's own box and place it at half size in your scene: http://127

Append them to the address, ?first=x&then=y: Option Effect --- --- ?test=1 Repeats a sample unlock every ten seconds, for positioning the source. Remove it afterwards. ?scale=2 Pins the card at that zoom instead of fitting it to the source. ?scale=app follows the scale set in Settings. ?duration=8000 Holds each card for that many milliseconds instead of the configured duration. ?sound=1 Plays the notification sound through the browser source, so it reaches the stream without capturing desktop audio. Off by default, since the app already plays it on your speakers. Tick Control audio via OBS on the source to put it in the mix. /obs/preset/Xbox/ Uses one named preset for the stream, whatever the desktop is set to. Any installed preset name works, including your own.

The page is blank between unlocks by design: nothing is drawn, so it costs no CPU until an achievement pops. It is local only. The page and the feed listen on 127.0.0.1, so nothing else on your network can reach them. Achievement icons are served from this machine for sources that keep their artwork locally (Goldberg, emulators, your own library art), and only for pictures a notification announced. One copy of AW Next serves the address: the one that started first. A second instance, or anything else on port 8082, leaves the source with nothing to connect to. Close the extra copy and the source reconnects within a few seconds. If the source stays blank on a real unlock, check that the test buttons work, then that the Websocket row is on.

Screenshot on unlock saves a picture of the screen a moment after an achievement pops, once the popup has finished appearing, so the notification is in the shot. Files land in <folder>\<game>\<achievement> - <date>.png. Open folder in the same row opens it, creating it first if needed. The folder defaults to Pictures\Achievement Watcher Next and can be changed. Achievements unlocking in the same second each keep their own file, and a game whose title Windows refuses as a folder name still gets its screenshots. On multi-monitor setups the souvenir captures the monitor the game is on, like the video clips; with no visible game window, it takes the monitor of the window in front, then the primary one.

HDR screenshots defaults to Automatic. At capture time, AW Next checks whether HDR is active on the display showing the game. If so, a one-shot helper captures an FP16 frame through Windows Graphics Capture and tone-maps its highlights into an SDR/sRGB PNG, then exits. With HDR off, Automatic and Off use the standard capture. Any helper failure (missing Windows support, a blocked capture, a timeout) also falls back to the standard screenshot, so the souvenir and the notification are not lost.

Video clip on unlock works like a console's trophy video. While a game AW Next tracks is running, the last seconds of play are kept in memory, already compressed by the graphics card's video encoder. When an achievement pops, the stretch around it is saved as an MP4 in <folder>\<game>\<achievement> - <date>.mp4, with the popup in the middle of it. The folder is Videos\Achievement Watcher Next unless you pick another. Achievements unlocking close together share one clip. sections.h: If a test or unlock does not appear
sections.x: Confirm notifications are enabled, and read the Notifications row of the game's Game Health panel. Check that the background tracker is running. For overlays, select a valid preset and test again outside an exclusive fullscreen game. Automatic already handles both cases. If a full-screen game or Do Not Disturb hides Windows notifications, enable Priority notifications and approve Windows' one-time request. Check Windows notification settings for AW Next. Open Settings → Advanced → Diagnostics and inspect the logs. If the problem remains, continue with Troubleshooting. -- Next: Presets and the Preset Designer - the look of the popup, and how to make your own. ← Documentation · Project home

A preset is the look of the in-game overlay popup: its layout, colours, motion and the way it paints a rare unlock or a 100% completion. Pick one under Settings → Notification → Preset, design your own in Settings → Notification presets, or import one somebody shared with you. sections.h: What is checked before anything is installed
sections.x: The rules are those of an .awpreset, since a theme file comes from somebody else's machine. Nothing inside one is run or evaluated; only its usertheme.json is read. Every path is checked against the package it came in, and the absolute paths SAN writes are read as filenames only. Only pictures, fonts and audio are taken out, by file type and under a size limit; an SVG that could run a script and a file that is not a font are refused. Every setting is checked for type and range. An import that fails leaves every preset you already have untouched.

Export and Import, in the Notification presets tab, move a preset between machines as one .awpreset file: the style, every image and font it uses, its designer settings and its metadata. The preset gallery collects these files: browse, download one and import it, or add yours. What a submission must be, and what is checked before it is listed, is in The community galleries. Export writes what the card is showing, under the name in the Name field: the design in the controls, saved or not, so a preset in progress can be shared without creating it first. An imported preset selected in Edit a preset is exported from disk as it is, since its look lives in files the controls cannot describe. Only the preset travels: no path from your machine, no account name, no setting of yours. Import asks for the file, checks it, and installs it under presets\Users Presets. sections.h: What is checked before anything is installed
sections.x: A package is validated whole and refused entirely, never part-installed, when: it is not a preset package, or its manifest is missing or malformed; it needs a newer AW Next than the one running, or a newer package format; it carries a file the format does not describe: a program, a script, or anything outside preset/ and sounds/; any path inside it points outside its own folder. Nothing inside a package is run or evaluated while it is checked or installed. The preset's page renders later, in the same sandboxed notification window as a bundled preset.

The manifest is kept beside the installed preset as aw-package.json. It tells the app the preset was imported and may be removed again, and carries the description and credit into the next export. A sound you imported yourself travels with the preset; a bundled sound does not, since the manifest names it and every install has it. Importing never changes the sound you have selected and never overwrites one you have: a different file of the same name arrives as name (2). The optional author field is filled only from the preset's own file, so nothing is credited to you unless you put it there. -- Next: Overlay - the in-game achievement list, which is separate from these popups. ← Documentation · Notifications · Project home

sections.h: Names, descriptions or artwork are missing
sections.x: Refresh while online so the app can retry its metadata sources. Confirm the game's platform identity; a wrong Steam AppID can return convincing but unrelated metadata. For Goldberg/GBE, a valid local schema can fill some missing text offline. Use the game's cover actions to retry or choose local artwork when automatic sources fail. A card titled with its bare Steam AppID means the name lookup came back empty while the artwork, which comes from the AppID alone, resolved. The next scan replaces the number once the lookup succeeds. DLC and update achievements show their owning group under the title (for example a "Hearts of Stone" tag), from Steam's own achievement sets or, for a game without them, from SteamHunters. Hidden achievement descriptions stay hidden when every available source omits them.

sections.h: A game update added achievements that aren't showing up
sections.x: A cached schema re-checks itself against Steam every 3 days, since Steam never announces new achievements. To pick them up at once, use Settings → Advanced → Recheck achievement lists, which works even with Automatic achievement data updates turned off. That switch, also under Settings → Advanced, stops only the periodic check and the repair of blank descriptions. Neither check removes existing achievements or unlocks. Turn it off only if you maintain steamcache by hand.

sections.h: An update is stuck on the same file
sections.x: Downloaded update files are kept between runs. If a download keeps failing on the same file, use Settings → Advanced → Clear caches and check for updates again. Only re-downloadable caches are deleted; settings, game data and logs stay. Updates normally download only the part of the installer that changed, and fall back to the full installer on their own if that fails. AW Next announces a new version with a Windows notification and a chip in the title bar, and clicking either opens the update window, which lists the release notes of every version you skipped. The notice stays until you close it and comes back after a game, never during one. The tray icon wears a blue dot meanwhile. Settings → Check for updates opens the window at once. Update refused. Every update is checked against the project's pinned signing certificate before it installs, not just any signature and not the SHA-512 pu

Confirm the background tracker is running. Open the game and read the Notifications row of its Game Health panel: it names the transport that delivered the last notification for that game, and why. Use the normal, rare and overlay tests under Settings → Notification. Confirm the delivery mode and selected preset. On Automatic, a missing overlay popup is often the intended fallback: see Notifications. Check Windows notification permissions for AW Next. If the issue happens only while playing or in full screen, turn on Priority notifications under Settings → Notification and accept the Windows permission prompt. Test the overlay outside exclusive fullscreen. Review the logs right after a failed test or unlock. If the library updates but no notification appears, the problem is the notification transport. If the library stays unchanged too, diagnose the source or save path first.

sections.h: The OBS browser source stays empty
sections.x: Press Preview under Settings → Notification → OBS browser source, or open http://127.0.0.1:8082/obs/?test=1. A sample card every ten seconds means the page and the feed work, and the problem is the source's settings in OBS. Nothing at all, not even a blank page: another copy of AW Next, or another program, holds port Only the copy that started first serves the address. A blank page is normal between unlocks. Use ?test=1 to see it draw. Check that Websocket @localhost:8082 is on under Settings → Notification → Transport: the source reads that feed. The card fills whatever size the source is. If it looks soft, give the source more pixels and place it smaller in the scene. See Show unlocks on stream (OBS) for the full setup.

sections.h: A game will not start from the Play button
sections.x: Some games need administrator rights, because their manifest or launcher asks for it. Windows refuses to start those the way AW Next normally starts a game and reports EACCES. AW Next then retries through the Windows shell, which raises the ordinary UAC prompt, so the game starts once you confirm. If that is refused too, AW Next offers to retry as administrator. Only the game is elevated, since an elevated AW Next would create files your normal account cannot rewrite. Dismissing the UAC prompt is treated as a decision, not an error.

AW Next follows the configured game executable and its process lifetime. If a launcher, helper or differently named binary starts instead: right-click the game and open its configuration; select the executable that remains active while playing; avoid launcher and crash-handler processes; restart the game after saving. A Java game that starts through javaw.exe and exits its own launcher is tracked through that Java process automatically. To correct a total that is already wrong, use Achievements & playtime → Edit playtime… (see Editing a game's playtime).

The PlayStation session has expired: connect the account again in Settings → Sources. PlayStation asks to slow down or Paused by PlayStation: Sony limits the request rate. Import again in a few minutes and it continues where it stopped. No trophy list on this account yet: the account has no trophy list to import.

sections.h: A Nemirtingas Epic game records nothing
sections.x: When a game folder holds the emulator (its EOSSDK library with a nepicesettings\NemirtingasEpicEmu.json beside it), the game's Game health tab shows an Epic emulator row: SavePath must be "appdata". The emulator writes achievements to %APPDATA%\NemirtingasEpicEmu, where AW Next reads them, only with that value; anything else keeps them in the game folder. The row warns when it is set to something else. Some games need the Epic launch arguments. Some EOS games sign in to the emulator, and so save an achievement, only when a launcher passes -epicapp=... and the others. While the emulator has saved nothing, the row offers Add the Epic launch arguments, which writes them into the game's launch settings from the config's AppId. A .bat that passes them works too. If the game crashes at launch with the emulator in place, turn its overlay plugin off ("Plugins": { "Overlay": { "Enabled": false }

sections.h: Ubisoft or Uplay R2 uses the wrong action
sections.x: Ubisoft games should get Ubisoft metadata and the Uplay R2 repair, not the Steam GBE action. Run a fresh folder scan and check the source icon. If the game is still misidentified, attach parser.log, the displayed source and IDs, and the game directory name to a report.

Packaged releases are signed with the project's own certificate, pinned by its exact thumbprint, not issued by a publicly trusted authority, so Windows SmartScreen may still warn. You never need to install the certificate. Before installing an update, AW Next checks that it is signed, that the signer is CN=Shirow, that the thumbprint matches one of the two the app has pinned, and that the file was not modified after signing. The SHA-512 published with a release cannot replace that check, since both would be replaced together. Optional emulator DLLs can also trigger heuristic detections. Download only from the official Releases page, and compare the installer with the SHA-512 in the matching latest.yml for a second check. Do not disable system-wide protection. Report a quarantined file from the official release to the antivirus vendor as a false positive.

Every published installer can be looked up on VirusTotal by its SHA-256: Open https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/<the hash it prints>. If the file is the published one, the report is already there. For the current release that is the 3.12.3 installer (277d0e7da8c2d04eb38eb43d3778cd595feb3901ebe653e88ebd521fd03cf7d1). The result lists what each engine thinks. A handful of heuristic detections on a build that bundles emulator files is the false positive described below. What matters is that the hash matches the file the releases page published.

This is the detection people actually hit, and it is a false positive. Recording achievements for a game with no store client running means putting a stand-in library beside it: the Steam emulator (GBE Fork) or a Ubisoft loader. Detection engines watch for exactly that, so they flag what the file does, not what it contains. Windows Defender quarantines every copy it can see at once: in the game folder, installed with AW Next, and in its cache. When it fires. sections.h: An antivirus reacts while AW Next runs
sections.x: Behaviour engines (Kaspersky's System Watcher, Bitdefender's Advanced Threat Defense) judge what a program does, not what it contains. AW Next starts no PowerShell for Windows notifications, toast sounds or the update signature check, and does not compile code into %TEMP%: screenshots use the native helper that ships with the app, and the notification check calls Windows directly. If your antivirus still reacts, note the exact detection name and report the file it names as a false positive. For Kaspersky that is opentip.kaspersky.com: look the file up by its hash, then Submit to reanalyze.

Use the tray icon (in the notification area) in case the app started hidden. End a stuck AW Next process, then launch it again. Remove ELECTRONRUNASNODE from the environment if it was set for development; it makes Electron start as plain Node. Check renderer.log and the main app log for the first error. Try Settings → General → Disable hardware acceleration if the UI stays visible long enough to change it.

Use this only after backing up data you want to keep: Exit AW Next fully from the tray. Rename %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next to Achievement Watcher Next.backup. Start the app and reproduce the issue with the new profile. If the issue disappears, restore only the data you need or attach the relevant configuration files to the report. Renaming keeps a way back; deleting does not.

Short answers to the usual questions. Each links to the guide that covers it.

sections.h: Do I need a Steam Web API key, or to sign in to Steam?
sections.x: No. Achievement lists come from a chain of public endpoints that needs no key, and nothing requires an account. Your own Steam unlocks are read from the stats Steam keeps on this PC, so a private profile works for every game played here. Connecting Steam is optional: it adds games played only on your other PCs, and Steam Family. See Connected accounts.

sections.h: Which platforms does it run on?
sections.x: Windows 10 and 11, and Linux (x64). Releases include their own runtime. Node.js is needed only to build from source.

sections.h: Does it run on Linux or the Steam Deck?
sections.x: On Linux, yes, as a beta: a native AppImage (never run through Wine) for GNOME and KDE Plasma, under Wayland or X11. It finds games run with Steam and Proton, Wine, Lutris, Heroic or Bottles, and updates itself from the same releases as the Windows app. On the Steam Deck, support is new and has not been checked on a real Deck. See Linux and the Steam Deck.

Yes. Turn on the RetroAchievements source, connect your account with its username and Web API key, and Import library brings in every game you played. New unlocks are announced while any RetroAchievements-enabled emulator runs. See RetroAchievements.

Yes. Connect your PlayStation account in Settings → Sources (you sign in on Sony's page) and your games and trophies are imported, with Sony's rate for each trophy. A game from another source that also came out on PlayStation shows the real platinum of its list. See Connected accounts.

sections.h: Do I have to connect an account?
sections.x: No. Steam, Epic, Xbox PC and PlayStation can each be connected to read what local files do not carry, and RetroAchievements asks for your username and Web API key. Every token and key is encrypted before it is stored on this PC. Everything else works without an account.

Yes, for local sources and anything already cached. Achievement names, descriptions and artwork are fetched once, then reused from %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\steamcache (~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next/steamcache on Linux).

sections.h: Do I lose anything by choosing Simple mode?
sections.x: No. Simple hides controls and never turns a feature off. Nothing that scans, watches or is stored changes, and switching back restores every control with its value. See Getting started.

sections.h: Can it show games I own but never installed, or unlocks from another PC?
sections.x: Yes. With the Steam source set to Owned, two switches in the Steam account card, Add the games you own and Add the games shared with you through Steam Family, list your whole library. Both are off by default because a large library makes the first scan much longer. With a Steam account connected, a game with nothing to read locally is read from your Steam profile (its game details must be public) and the answer is cached for six hours. See Connected accounts.

Check that its source is enabled in Settings → Sources, run Smart Find under Settings → Folders, and turn off Show installed games only to see whether the game is known but no longer installed. The full checklist is in Troubleshooting.

That game has no achievement set. It stays launchable and keeps tracking playtime, and it is left out of completion statistics instead of counting as 0%. Its tile shows artwork where the progress bar would be. Settings → Appearance → Library tiles → Bar of games without achievements brings the bar back.

sections.h: A game shows 0% although I have unlocked achievements
sections.x: The game has a schema but no unlock file at runtime. Open its Game Health panel: it names the missing piece and offers only the repairs that apply.

sections.h: Why does the same game appear twice?
sections.x: It was found through two sources. Merge Duplicates in Settings → General combines them. If one entry is a stale save folder for a game you now own elsewhere, blacklist it.

sections.h: A game update added achievements and I do not see them
sections.x: A cached list re-checks itself every 3 days. To pick up new ones now, use Settings → Advanced → Recheck achievement lists, which works even with Automatic achievement data updates off. Neither check removes anything already cached.

sections.h: A game was matched to the wrong Steam release
sections.x: Right-click it and choose Set AppID manually.... The AppID is written to steamappid.txt and remembered for that install folder. See Set a game's AppID by hand.

sections.h: Nothing appears when I unlock something
sections.x: Start with the Notifications row of that game's Game Health panel, which names the transport that last delivered and why. Then follow If a test or unlock does not appear.

sections.h: The overlay popup does not show in one particular game
sections.x: That game is probably in exclusive fullscreen, where an always-on-top popup cannot be drawn. On Automatic, AW Next sends that unlock as a Windows notification shown over the game. A game in legacy exclusive mode lets nothing through: switch it to borderless. See how Automatic decides.

sections.h: Notifications are hidden while I play
sections.x: That is Windows' Do Not Disturb. Turn on Priority notifications and approve Windows' one-time request. See Priority Windows notifications.

sections.h: Can I change how the popup looks, or share a design?
sections.x: Yes. Ten presets ship with the app, the Preset Designer builds your own with ordinary controls, and any preset exports to one .awpreset file. See Presets and the Preset Designer.

sections.h: Can I put unlocks on my stream?
sections.x: Yes, with a Browser source in OBS. Capturing the popup as a window cannot work, since it exists for one unlock and is gone before OBS lists it, so AW Next serves the same popup as a page. The address is in Settings → Notification → OBS browser source. See Show unlocks on stream (OBS).

sections.h: Is the overlay the same thing as the popup?
sections.x: No. The popup is a one-shot notification styled by a preset. The overlay is the full achievement list you open with Ctrl+Shift+K while a game runs. See the Overlay guide.

sections.h: On Linux, Ctrl+Shift+K does nothing in my game
sections.x: Under Wayland, AW Next cannot see keys pressed while a native Wayland window has focus, such as a Linux game in Wayland mode or Proton with its Wayland driver. Bind a key in your desktop's keyboard settings to /home/you/.local/bin/achievement-watcher --toggle-overlay, with your user name in place of you. AW Next keeps that command pointing at the current AppImage, so the shortcut survives updates. See Overlay shortcut.

sections.h: Does AW Next modify my games, or send anything off my PC?
sections.x: Only when you ask. Reading achievements is read-only. The emulator repair tools (a game's right-click Emulator & tools submenu and Settings → Emulators) write to a game folder, always after a confirmation and with a backup. Use them only with games you own. Beyond read-only lookups and what a connected account sends back, nothing leaves this PC. See What leaves this PC.

sections.h: My antivirus flagged or removed a file
sections.x: It is almost certainly the Steam emulator or a Ubisoft loader, and a false positive: these files stand in for a game's Steam or Ubisoft library, which is the behaviour detection engines look for. Nothing is written unless you ran a repair, opened Settings → Emulators, or turned on automatic repair. Allow the file your antivirus named, or exclude %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\cache. Never switch protection off. See Troubleshooting → Antivirus.

sections.h: Windows SmartScreen warns about the installer
sections.x: Releases are signed with the project's own certificate, pinned by thumbprint, rather than a commercial one, so SmartScreen may ask for confirmation. You never need to install that certificate: the in-app updater checks the signer, the pinned thumbprint and that the file was not modified after signing before it installs anything. Download only from the official releases page. To check an installer yourself, run Get-FileHash <installer> -Algorithm SHA256 and open https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/<hash>. The current release is 3.12.3. See Troubleshooting → Checking a release yourself.

sections.h: On Linux, why does a keyring prompt appear?
sections.x: AW Next encrypts its sign-in tokens with a key held by your desktop keyring (GNOME Keyring or KDE Wallet). With automatic login the keyring stays locked, so the desktop asks you to unlock or create one when AW Next starts. Cancelling is safe: the app keeps working and the prompt returns at the next start. See Keyring prompt.

sections.h: Where is my data, does updating lose it, and how big are updates?
sections.x: Everything is in %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next (~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next on Linux), and installing a newer build keeps it. The first launch after upgrading imports an older Achievement Watcher folder without modifying or deleting it. Updates download only what changed since your installed version, and fall back to a full download by themselves if that fails. See Updates and existing data.

sections.h: How do I move to a new PC, or back up my setup?
sections.x: Settings → Advanced → Profile backup → Export profile… writes your settings, library choices, presets, themes, covers and playtime to one .awbackup file. Install AW Next on the new PC, choose Restore profile…, and it is applied at the next start; the files it replaces are kept. Sign-ins are never saved, so connect Steam, Epic, Xbox, PlayStation and RetroAchievements again. See Profile backup.

Yes. The portable ZIP keeps the app and its data in one folder and checks the same release feed as the installed app. It never downloads or runs the installer: it offers the release page when a newer version is out, and extracting the new archive over the old folder keeps your data.
Closing the window keeps AW Next in the system tray so tracking continues. Use the tray menu to exit.

sections.h: How does this differ from Achievement Watcher 2.x?
sections.x: AW Next continues it with a modern runtime and a large pass on compatibility, reliability and features. See the Comparison.

sections.h: Can it get me games, keys or accounts?
sections.x: No, and the issue tracker cannot help with that either. AW Next contains no game files and does not bypass online ownership checks.

sections.h: I found a bug or have an idea
sections.x: Open an issue with the app version, your Windows version (or Linux distribution and desktop), the source involved and the relevant logs. Report a suspected vulnerability privately through the security policy. For a question, or help before you know it is a bug, ask on the Discord server. -- Still stuck? Troubleshooting goes through each symptom in order. ← Documentation · Project home

AW Next runs on Linux (x64) as a native app, never through Wine. It follows games run through Steam and Proton, Wine, Lutris, Heroic or Bottles, native Linux games and the supported emulators, with the same library, popups, overlay and playtime as on Windows. The Linux build is a beta. It was tested on GNOME and KDE Plasma, in Wine and Proton prefixes and with test games, but not on many real machines: a real Steam Deck, real gamepads, every launcher and every scene release. If something does not work, an issue with your distribution, desktop and logs helps most.

Open the latest release and download Achievement.Watcher.<version>.AppImage. Put it in a folder of your own, such as ~/Applications, and make it executable: in the file manager, Properties → Allow executing file as program, or in a terminal: Start it and follow the first-run guide as on Windows (see Getting started). An AppImage needs FUSE 2, which some distributions, Ubuntu 24.04 among them, no longer install by default. If the file does not start, install it: libfuse2t64 on Ubuntu 24.04 and later, libfuse2 on older Ubuntu and Debian, fuse-libs on Fedora, fuse2 on Arch. On its first start AW Next adds itself to the application menu. Settings → General → Launch at startup starts it, hidden in the tray, at each login. Settings, caches, playtime and logs live in ~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next.

The AppImage updates itself from the same GitHub releases as the Windows app. A new version is announced by a desktop notification and the title-bar chip, and it asks before downloading. It then checks the file against the SHA-512 digest published with the release (latest-linux.yml), replaces the old AppImage and restarts. If a game is running, the update waits until it closes. Your data stays where it was. The new file has the new version in its name. The Launch at startup entry and the ~/.local/bin/achievement-watcher command follow it. A launcher you made yourself that names the AppImage file still points at the old name, so point it at that command instead.

AW Next is tested on GNOME and KDE Plasma, under Wayland and X11 (Ubuntu 24.04 with GNOME 46 and Plasma 5.27), and on Fedora 44 with GNOME 50, Plasma 6.7, Hyprland 0.56 and COSMIC 1.0, in a virtual machine. Other desktops may work but have not been tried. Wayland. AW Next restarts itself once through XWayland at startup so its popups and overlay can stay above games, which run as X11 windows under Wine and Proton. Hyprland and COSMIC start XWayland by default. Without it (xwayland.enabled = false on Hyprland), AW Next stays a native Wayland app: the library, tray and notifications work, but the compositor places the popups and the overlay like any window, and a popup takes the keyboard from the game while it shows. Tray. KDE and COSMIC show the tray icon as is. GNOME needs the AppIndicator extension, which Ubuntu ships turned on. Hyprland needs a bar with a tray, such as Waybar with its

Screenshots and clips of each unlock work on X11 and on Wayland. Clips are recorded by gpu-screen-recorder with the graphics card when it is installed. If you choose it in Settings, AW Next's own software recorder saves WebM files instead and shows what it cost. On Wayland, the first screenshot makes the desktop ask whether apps may take screenshots (GNOME 47 and later, KDE Plasma 6, COSMIC and Hyprland). AW Next waits a few seconds for the answer, then skips that shot, and the ones of unlocks that come while the question is open. Click Allow, since Enter picks Deny on GNOME and Hyprland, and the next screenshots are taken without a word. If you deny it, AW Next takes no screenshots and does not ask again. To be asked again at the next screenshot, run: The software recorder captures the screen through the desktop's screen-sharing dialog, which comes back each time a game starts and, on C

Ctrl+Shift+K opens the overlay while a Wine or Proton game has focus. Under Wayland, AW Next cannot see a key pressed while a native Wayland window has focus, such as a Linux game in Wayland mode or Proton with its Wayland driver. There is no in-game hotkey for those games. A shortcut from your desktop's keyboard settings does not depend on that. Have it run this command, with you replaced by your user name (GNOME does not expand ~, so write the full path): It opens or closes the overlay of the copy already running and starts nothing else. The command exists from the first start of the AppImage, and AW Next refreshes it at every start, so it follows updates. GNOME: Settings → Keyboard → View and Customize Shortcuts → Custom Shortcuts → Add Shortcut. Name it, paste the command, then press the keys you want. KDE Plasma 6: System Settings → Keyboard → Shortcuts → Add New → Command or Script

The few secrets AW Next keeps (Steam, Epic, Xbox and PlayStation sign-in tokens, the RetroAchievements key, an emulator Steam password) are encrypted with a key held by your desktop keyring: GNOME Keyring or KDE Wallet. Hyprland has none of its own and uses the one installed, which starts when AW Next first asks for it. With automatic login, the keyring is not unlocked when your session starts. The first time AW Next needs it, the desktop asks you to unlock it, or to create one if there is none; KDE opens the KDE Wallet assistant. Answer it and AW Next goes on. If you cancel, AW Next keeps working, says once that your connections are not protected, and the desktop asks again at the next start. The prompt never blocks the app: tracking and notifications run while it is open.

AW Next finds the Steam client whether it comes from your distribution (steam-installer, steam), from Flathub or as a Snap, along with its library folders on other disks and each game's Proton prefix. With two Steam clients installed, it follows the one started last. Unlocks of games Steam itself runs are read from Steam's own files, as on Windows. AW Next pops them up only once Settings → Notification → Steam client games is on, since Steam shows its own popup for them.

Every source is read inside the game's prefix, its Windows registry included: a game with a Steam emulator (Goldberg, GBE Fork and the others in Compatible sources), a Ubisoft or GOG save, and so on. Smart Find searches your home folder, your other disks and every prefix it knows. Lutris and Bottles: the games and programs they installed are listed with their prefix. Heroic: Epic games installed through Heroic are recognised as Epic games. Plain Wine: the default ~/.wine prefix and any prefix folder you add. Native Linux games with Goldberg or GBE Fork (libsteamapi.so) are read from their Linux save folders. Play starts a game through the launcher it belongs to (Steam, Lutris, Heroic), and playtime is counted from the game's process. The emulator repairs of Game Health work from the AppImage and write inside the game's prefix, with a backup as always.

RPCS3, shadPS4, RetroArch and Xenia are found in their Linux folders; RPCS3 and shadPS4 also when they come from Flathub. RetroAchievements unlocks are announced whatever the emulator, once the source is connected.

Steam Deck support is new and has not been checked on a real Deck. What it is meant to do: In Desktop Mode, AW Next is the same AppImage as on any Linux desktop. The first window fits the Deck's 1280x800 screen, and games on the microSD card are found. With Launch at startup on, AW Next also runs in Game Mode: it starts as a background service once Steam is up. Game Mode shows no desktop notifications, so AW Next draws each unlock as its own popup over the game, from the top-left corner. SteamOS's performance overlay may hide that popup. The Decky plugin in the repository's decky/ folder sends each unlock to Steam's own notifications, which Game Mode always draws. While it listens, AW Next keeps its own popup off, so you see one notification. Without the plugin the popup is the fallback. For now you install it by hand: build it (npm install, then npm run build) and copy it to ~/homebrew/

Include your distribution, desktop (GNOME or KDE, Wayland or X11), how the game runs (Steam with Proton, Lutris, Heroic, Bottles, Wine) and the files in ~/.config/Achievement Watcher Next/logs. -- Next: Troubleshooting, for discovery, progress, notification and playtime problems. ← Documentation · Getting started · Project home

These tools are under Settings → Advanced or in a game's right-click menu. The Advanced tab exists only while the interface is in Advanced mode: switch the Interface control at the top of Settings if you do not see it. Nothing is lost by switching back. Setup & maintenance; the other sections fold away below it

Tool What it does --- --- Fix all detected games Runs the matching repair (Steam/GBE Fork or Ubisoft/Uplay R2) over every compatible detected game with a known install folder. This rebuilds games that already have a setup. Disable hardware acceleration Turns off GPU acceleration when the window or overlay misbehaves. Needs a restart. Clear caches Deletes only re-downloadable caches: update files, the Steam/Ubisoft schema and icon cache, and downloaded emulator-fix tools. Settings, saves, backups and manually placed files are never touched. Recheck achievement lists Checks Steam for achievements added by a game update. This runs every 3 days; the button forces it now. Automatic achievement data updates On by default. Off stops that recheck and the blank-description repair, for anyone who maintains steamcache by hand. Recheck achievement lists still works while it is off. Source-specific r

Versions, and one click to the logs and data folders The Diagnostics card prints the app, Electron, Node and Chrome versions, and opens the logs folder, the data folder or an update check. Export logs (.zip) bundles every log file into one archive while the app runs; copying them by hand is unreliable because the processes writing them never stop. Your user name and any key, token or password are masked in the archive, not in the logs on disk. See Troubleshooting for what a bug report needs.

Export profile and Restore profile, under Settings → Advanced Export profile… saves your settings, library choices, presets, themes, covers, custom backgrounds, GBE restore points and playtime to one .awbackup file, for a reinstall or a new PC. Sign-ins, caches and logs are never saved, so you sign in again to Epic, Steam, Xbox, PlayStation and RetroAchievements afterwards. Restore profile… checks the whole file first and applies it at the next start. The files it replaces are kept, and a failed restore puts everything back.

A game removed from the library with Blacklist is listed here with the ID it was blacklisted under, and can be restored one by one. Use the blacklist for a stray folder that the scan keeps finding but that is not a game.

Reset achievements, on the game's page beside the playtime or in its right-click menu, sends every achievement back to locked so you can play the game through again. AW Next announces them as new when they unlock. Reset sits beside the completion count on the game's own page Every file involved is backed up first to %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\backups\achievements\<appid>\<date>\, and the confirmation lists the exact files before anything is touched. A file whose backup fails is skipped, not cleared. Source What a reset does --- --- Steam emulators (Goldberg / GBE and compatible layouts, including Goldberg SocialClub and Uplay R2) Removes the achievement save. The emulator writes a fresh one at the next unlock. RPCS3 Removes TROPUSR.DAT. The trophy list (TROPCONF.SFM) is left alone. ShadPS4 Relocks the trophies inside TROP.XML, which also holds the trophy list, so the file is edit

Right-click an unlocked achievement on the game's page and choose Re-lock this achievement to play for that one again. Only that achievement goes back to locked: its flag, unlock time and progress in the emulator's save, its counter when the save links one to it, and AW Next's own record, so it is announced as new when you earn it. The confirmation lists the files and every file is backed up first, as for a reset; Restore an achievement backup puts it back. Close the game first. An emulator keeps its unlocks in memory and writes them back when the game exits, which would undo the change, so AW Next refuses while a game is running. It works with the text saves of the Steam emulators (Goldberg and GSE, CODEX, RUNE, OnlineFix, RLD!, 3DM, ALI213, TENOKE, Hoodlum, RAZOR1911, CreamAPI), UniverseLAN, Nemirtingas, Uplay R1 and R2, GreenLuma and LumaPlay on Windows, and the console saves of RPCS3

Forget this game..., in the right-click menu, clears everything AW Next keeps about a game: its achievement saves (backed up first, as a reset does), play time, cached achievement list and icons, per-game settings, and the emulator configuration AW Next wrote into its folder. The confirmation lists each part first. The next scan finds the game again as a new one. Remove from list only hides a game.

Game settings → Rename…, in the right-click menu, sets the name a game is shown under: on its tile and screen, in search and sorting, in notifications, and in the folders screenshots and clips are saved to. Search still finds the game by its original name. Leave the field empty, or pick Restore the original name, to go back. The name is kept per game in cfg/gameTitles.json, so it survives rescans and is part of a profile backup. Cover lookups and game matching use the original name. Settings → General → Game titles in my language, on by default, shows Steam games under the title Steam gives them in your achievement language (the game's own language when it has one). Covers follow the same language. Steam's local catalogue answers for games your Steam client knows; the rest are asked once, in batches, and checked again after a month. A name you set yourself always wins.

Achievements & playtime → Edit playtime…, in the right-click menu, replaces a game's total playtime, for example one carried over from another tracker or one that missed sessions. Type hours (12.5) or hours and minutes (12h30 or 12:30). The date of the last session is kept, and AW Next adds later sessions to the new total. A game you own on Steam never goes below the playtime Steam reports: the next scan raises a lower total back to Steam's.

sections.h: A different achievement language for one game
sections.x: Game settings → Achievement language, in the right-click menu, shows one game's achievements and notifications in another language than the rest of the library. Same as the app goes back to the global choice.

The + beside the library search adds a game from a title and an executable, with an optional platform and Steam AppID. Use it for a game no source detects: a standalone build, a portable install, or an emulator you launch yourself. A manually added game: is launchable and tracks playtime like any other entry; shows No achievements if it has none, and is left out of completion statistics instead of counting as 0%; can adopt a Steam achievement schema later by adding the AppID, without being recreated; keeps guarded per-game diagnostics, while destructive actions stay hidden. Manually added folders carry a compact icon in the Folders list, to tell them from the locations Smart Find discovered.

sections.h: Set a game's AppID by hand
sections.x: Right-click a game whose folder name matches several Steam releases, so the automatic match picked the wrong one, and choose Set AppID manually.... An .awpreset holds the preset's document and stylesheet, its images, fonts and sound, and the designer settings behind it. Nothing about your machine. An .awtheme holds colours, gradients, fits, effect settings and any background image you picked, and nothing else: no stylesheet, markup or script. An image travels as bytes under a name built from its layer, never as a path out of your pictures folder. The full list is in the .awtheme format. A user stylesheet theme cannot be exported. A .css you dropped into %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\themes is not an .awtheme, and Export refuses it. Share the .css itself.

Everything inside a package is redistributed to everyone who downloads it, so it must be yours to redistribute: Your own artwork, or something under a licence that allows it. A wallpaper you found is usually neither, and neither is a font you bought. Nothing with a logo, a watermark or baked-in text. A theme is a look, not a placement. Nothing that would not pass as a desktop background at work. A theme made of colours alone is welcome and the easiest kind to accept.

The name on a card is whatever the Credit box ends up saying. It starts as the author the app recorded when you exported, so it is usually right. Change it if you go by something else, or empty it and the card carries no name. A maintainer can add a link to your profile when approving it. Everything listed in either gallery is published under CC BY 4.0. By submitting you agree to that, confirm it is your own work and that everything inside it is yours to give.

A submission has to pass two layers. The app's own reader. app/util/presetPackage.js and app/util/themePackage.js, the modules that run on Import, validate the package: the manifest, the format version, the minimum app version, every path inside it, the file types, the sizes and the entry point. The gallery service uses those files verbatim, so a rule added there applies here on the next build, and nothing can be listed that the app would refuse. The gallery's own limits, which a private import does not need: --- --- File name Lower-case letters, digits and dashes, 2 to 48 characters, built by the service from the name Package 4 MB for a preset, 8 MB for a theme Picture Rendered by the service, once per state, and refused if one comes out outside the size a listing serves (500 KB at most each) Name Unique in its gallery, since two entries with one name collide on import Nothing in a pack

Someone else's work, unless they said yes and you credit them. Assets you cannot redistribute. A popup posing as something else: a system dialog, an advert, an address to visit. An advert, logo or call to action baked into a background image. A palette that makes text unreadable. A near-duplicate of something already listed. A refusal keeps the checksum and deletes the bytes, so sending the same file again is recognised instead of queued twice.

Send the newer file the same way, with the version inside the package raised, and say in the description that it replaces an earlier card so a maintainer can take that one down. To have an entry removed, open an issue and say which card it is.

Electron's bundled Node runs both processes. The installed app ships no second Node or NW.js executable.

AW Next ships for Windows (installer and portable ZIP) and Linux (an x64 AppImage). Linux code never changes what Windows does: it sits behind process.platform or the host layer below. The library paints from cache/librarysnapshot before discovery starts, so the scan is not on the path to the first frame. Four rules bound its cost: Read a folder once per pass. app/util/dirCache.js memoizes directory listings for one discovery. The memo is closed afterward, so a repair always sees the real folder. Skip an unchanged install folder. app/util/exeCandidateCache.js remembers a game folder's executable candidates, keyed by its timestamps, under cache/discovery/. Do not scan while a game runs. The background pass holds until the game exits. A ceiling on held passes keeps a background process mistaken for a game from suspending it silently. Prove the disk is unchanged before walking it again. The new-install poll compares the timestamps of the folders the last discovery read (app/util/dirFingerprint.js) and skips the pass when none moved. Database and registry sources are invis

Parsers normally expose a scan function and an initDebug hook. The aggregator normalizes their results; they render nothing. When adding a source: keep the source's native identity instead of forcing every item into a Steam AppID; distinguish installed state from leftover achievement data; return partial data when safe instead of blacklisting a game after one transient failure; cache network results with a bounded lifetime; make missing optional files a normal empty state; keep watcher and parser rules aligned so the library and live notifications observe the same files.

Each side has its own list, so a new one touches both: The reader. A small module of its own in app/parser/ that requires nothing from the rest of the app, so the Watchdog can load it. List it in asarUnpack in app/electron-builder.yml; test/core/sharedAppModules.test.js fails otherwise. Library roots. Add the folder to addHostRoots in app/parser/saveRoots.js as envPath('APPDATA', '<Folder>'). It is then probed on every host. Library label and file. steam.scan() in app/parser/steam.js names the source from the folder path (an unrecognised folder shows as Steam-emulator). getAchievementsFromFile() in the same file lists the save file names it reads and turns each format into shared { Achieved, UnlockTime } e

Some locale bindings depend on DOM order, so changing settings markup can shift text onto the wrong control even when the JSON keys are right.
