How AW Next discovers, reads and repairs Goldberg/GBE-compatible achievement data. For setup steps, use the user guide.

The schema and the runtime state are two files with the same name: Local schema Runtime save --- --- --- Path <game>\steamsettings\achievements.json %APPDATA%\GSE Saves\<appid>\achievements.json or %APPDATA%\Goldberg SteamEmu Saves\<appid>\achievements.json JSON shape Array of achievement definitions Object keyed by achievement API name Purpose Names, descriptions, hidden state and icon paths Earned state and unlock time Main reader app/parser/goldberg.js app/parser/steam.js and app/parser/achievements.js The schema follows the GBE example shape: hidden is the string "0" or "1". Icon paths are relative to steamsettings. The normal GBE runtime shape is: The shared parser also accepts the field names of other compatible local save formats.

The default roots are under %APPDATA%: GSE Saves\<appid> for GBE Fork; Goldberg SteamEmu Saves\<appid> for classic Goldberg. A missing runtime file is not an error: no unlock state has been written yet. A custom save path must resolve into a watched root or be added as a user folder. A GBE Fork install also creates the classic Goldberg folder (and the reverse), so both can exist for one appid. Discovery then compares how many achievements each file has recorded (steam.goldbergSaveWeight, used in app/parser/achievements.js) and reads the one that holds the unlocks. It corrects an earlier choice if a later pass finds more progress in the other folder.

Applying a setup calls seedRuntimeSave, which writes <root>\<appid>\achievements.json with every achievement locked, so a fixed game shows its list before it has run. That file looks like a real save with no unlocks, so runtimeSaveSeed drops a .aw-seed.json marker beside it with the size and CRC of what was written. While the file matches, only AW Next has touched it; the emulator's first store ends the match. inspectSaveState exposes this as save.seeded, the diagnosis raises SAVESEEDEDNOTWRITTEN instead of SAVEPRESENT, and the health panel does not count the placeholder as progress. The marker lives in the save folder, not userData, so it survives a portable install, a userData migration and a second AW Next on the same machine.

app/parser/goldberg.js goes by local files, not by product name: configs..ini under steamsettings identifies the GBE-style configuration; a populated steamsettings without those INI files is treated as classic Goldberg-compatible; a replaced Steam API DLL identifies an unconfigured install even before steamsettings exists; a real steamappid.txt beats a name-based AppID guess. Install discovery walks the configured game libraries to a bounded depth. It can surface an installed game before its first runtime save, attach the install path to a game already found from saves, and mark incomplete installs for later repair. Name-based AppID matching strips common version and repack suffixes, then ranks exact, token and fuzzy candidates. Only confident matches are written automatically; an ambiguous one needs a user choice.

diagnose reports schema and runtime state independently, so an empty save is never misreported as a broken schema. It checks: emulator type and steamsettings location; whether steamsettings sits beside the emulator DLL (SETTINGSNOTBESIDEDLL); on-disk AppID against the resolved game; schema validity and missing achievement API names; blank descriptions and missing icons; GBE configuration and custom save paths; whether a runtime save exists, how many achievements are earned, and whether the file is still AW Next's seeded placeholder (SAVESEEDEDNOTWRITTEN); whether steaminterfaces.txt is present, and if not whether an original Steam API DLL is still on disk to generate it from (NOSTEAMINTERFACES, NOSTEAMINTERFACESUNRECOVERABLE). Both are info level: GSE answers from its built-in interface versions without the file, which suits most titles, and a release that shipped its own emulator over t

A packaged Unreal build does not load steamapi(64).dll from beside the executable. Its engine loads one by explicit path from Engine\Binaries\ThirdParty\Steamworks\Steamv<version>\Win64, six levels below the build root and outside the game folder when a library anchored the game on its project subfolder. Emulator walks are depth-limited and cannot see that DLL. app/util/unrealLayout.js probes that one fixed path instead of deepening the walks. The engine's folder leads the install and repair targets, and UNREALENGINEDLLUNCONFIGURED reports a setup anywhere else. Every packaged build ships Valve's own DLL there, so presence proves nothing: it counts as a setup only when the DLL carries the emulator marker or a steamsettings sits beside it. describeRuntimeDlls (app/parser/gbeInstaller.js) reports, per folder, the DLL's size and mtime, whether it is an emulator, whether it is the supported

repair builds a normalized schema from the best available achievement metadata and updates the GBE configuration with section-aware INI edits. Unknown sections, comments and existing keys are kept where possible. A repair may: write or refresh achievements.json; download normal and locked icons into steamsettings\images; create steamappid.txt when it is missing; set DLC behavior in configs.app.ini; set required main options in configs.main.ini; set account name, language and a valid save path in configs.user.ini. When the diagnosed folder has no emulator DLL beside it, the repair writes into the DLL's folder (the one beside the game executable when several DLLs are on disk). The confirmation says where the files go; the original folder is left untouched. An existing rich schema is kept when it has more useful progress metadata than the replacement, and so are existing Steam IDs and curat

GBE supports a general unlock flag and explicit DLC enumeration: When data is available and Manage DLC ownership is on, AW Next writes both. The switch is under Settings → Steam / GBE Fork → Emulator setup and is off by default: unlocking every DLC has nothing to do with reading achievements, and it overwrites a file some repacks or players curate by hand. Explicit IDs let games enumerate DLC, while unlockall=1 covers ownership checks that query a specific ID. Existing entries are merged, not discarded.

The relevant GBE section is: The account name and language follow AW Next settings only when Write account name and language is on under Settings → Steam / GBE Fork → Emulator setup. It is off by default and independent of DLC ownership and automatic repair. With it off, a repair started by hand from Game Health fills in the emulator's defaults (Player / english); a value already in the file is never replaced. The name comes from the Emulator identity card, or from the AW Next profile name when that field is empty. An existing accountsteamid is kept, because changing it can redirect the emulator to a different save identity; only a valid Steam ID typed in that card, with the switch on, replaces it. A save folder chosen on that card is written as [user::saves] localsavepath whatever the switch, the setup prepares that folder instead of GSE Saves, and the Watchdog watches it. A relative fo

app/parser/gbeInstaller.js downloads a Windows release from Detanup01/gbefork into the local cache and keeps the matching 32-bit and 64-bit DLLs with their generateinterfaces tools. The cache is reused; the release endpoint is not queried on every scan. installDlls picks the architecture already present in each game directory, keeps the original DLL as a one-time .bak, and installs only a matched runtime set. AW Next replaces the Steam API DLL with a standalone one; ColdClient is not part of the current setup. Where "Switch to the supported emulator" ran, Game Health offers a link that puts the crack's own files back. Advanced schema generation is separate. app/parser/genEmuConfig.js uses the maintained gseforktools generator and merges its output into the game's steamsettings instead of replacing the directory.

app/parser/steamless.js unpacks SteamStub after explicit confirmation and keeps the original executable as .steamstub.bak. app/parser/apiCheckBypass.js is an opt-in compatibility path for games that re-check the original Steam API after a replacement. It is off by default. Neither path bypasses online ownership or server-side checks.

Normal scanning can discover installs and fill a missing schema without replacing runtime DLLs. The full background emulator setup is controlled by emulator.autoApplyNewGames and is off by default. Background attempts are keyed by game and content version, so an unchanged broken install is not rewritten on every scan. A manual diagnosis or repair is always available for a retry.

Never treat the schema file as proof of an unlock. Never write an uncertain AppID automatically. Back up before replacing a DLL, executable or populated configuration. Keep unknown INI content and stable account identity. Keep install discovery bounded and skip dependency, redist and tool directories. Keep manual and background setup paths on the same repair functions. Install into every folder the game may load the DLL from, and treat a setup as done only when they all carry the supported build. Prefer a safe partial result over hiding a game after a transient metadata failure. -- Next: Architecture - where this code runs, and which process owns which responsibility. ← Documentation · Setup guide · Project home
How AW Next identifies, repairs and reads Ubisoft games running the Goldberg Uplay emulator. For contributors and for debugging a setup. The user guide is Uplay setup.

A game loads only the Uplay API generation its executable was linked against. AW Next reads the executable's imports and repairs that generation, never the other. R2 (roughly 2019 onward) R1 (older titles) --- --- --- Loader upcr2loader64.dll / upcr2loader.dll uplayr1loader64.dll / uplayr1loader.dll Config files upcr2.ini and uplayr2.ini upcr1.ini and uplayr1.ini Config section [Settings] [Uplay] Own save root %APPDATA%\Goldberg UplayEmu Saves\<uplayId> %APPDATA%\R1 UplayEmu Saves\<uplayId> Loader log upcr2.log upcr1.log Modern loaders redirect achievement data to %APPDATA%\GSE Saves\<steamAppid>; older builds keep their own root. AW Next reads and watches all three.

The repair stops unless it can: identify the Ubisoft game and its installation; match it to a Steam release, from app/assets/uplay-steam.json or from a choice the user confirms; map every Steam achievement name to a Ubisoft objective ID; prove the exact loader name and x86/x64 architecture the game uses. An official Ubisoft loader with a similar filename is therefore never replaced, and official Ubisoft Connect installs are never selected from a DLL name alone.

In order: cfg/uplay-r2-mappings.json: pairings resolved or confirmed earlier, read first. app/assets/uplay-steam.json: the shipped snapshot. The Ubisoft to Steam resolver shared with artwork and rarity. It reads Ubisoft's public product catalogue (no account; official name and boxart per product ID) and the community UPLAYGAMEID list, then pairs by title under a strict rule: a single Steam game with the same title. Spelling slips and edition or storefront suffixes are tolerated. An older game is never taken for a newer one whose name contains it, and an edition Steam sells under its own AppID is never folded into the base game. An interactive choice among ranked Steam catalogue matches. A steamappid.txt in the game folder is shown first as a hint and never trusted without confirmation. The Ubisoft product ID does not depend on the map. The game states it to the loader at startup, so AW N

The loader rebuilds each key as AchKeyPrefix followed by the objective ID as a plain number, so the generated schema drops leading zeros: Steam's 001 becomes 1. A game whose names would then collide (two achievements on one objective ID) is reported unsupported instead of configured with an achievement missing. When a Steam name carries no objective number, AW Next uses the achievement definitions Ubisoft Connect caches for any product whose achievements page it has shown, joined on the title in any language the archive ships. That makes titles such as Brawlhalla or The Crew 2 configurable; without the cached archive they stay unsupported. Opening the game's achievements page in Ubisoft Connect once fills that cache.

The loader proved by the game: one of the integrated DLLs (app/resources/uplayR2/ and app/resources/uplayR1/, checked by hash, PE architecture and achievement capability) or a DLL the user imported (no known hash needed, but it must be a valid, achievement-capable loader with a coherent name and architecture). achievementsschema.json. Both config files of that generation. Every changed DLL, schema and INI is snapshotted under <game>\.aw-backups\<timestamp>\. Validation runs after the write and restores the snapshot if anything fails. An identical repair is a no-op. One transaction backs the context menu, Game Health, automatic repair, Fix All and the batch button. A recovery archive sits beside the integrated DLLs in case an antivirus removes one. When both are gone or the archive is quarantined mid-read, the app reports an antivirus problem and offers to allow the folder and restore the

Game Health reads upcr1.log / upcr2.log beside the loader to tell apart the two reasons nothing unlocks: the game never asked for an achievement, or it asked for an objective number the schema does not carry. Diagnostic logging is therefore on by default. The loader appends forever, so AW Next deletes the log past 25 MB.

Some titles ask for the Ubisoft session first. The loader answers from a [Settings] Ticket key it leaves empty, the game reads that as signed out and never calls the achievement API (Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora does this). Only when the log proves it does Game Health offer Enable achievements offline, which writes a placeholder shaped like a session token into that key and nothing else. No account is involved and nothing is sent. It is never automatic, since the emulator's authors warn a non-legitimate token breaks some games. R1 builds do not read the key (their TickedId is unrelated), so it is never offered there, and a Ticket line an older AW Next wrote into an R1 folder is removed. -- ← Documentation · Uplay setup · Project home

An application theme travels as one file. .awtheme is a zip with a fixed layout, written and read by app/util/themePackage.js, the only code that unpacks one. This page is the format itself. Sending a theme to the gallery is covered in The community galleries; what themes are and how the editor works is in Advanced. A notification theme imported from Steam Achievement Notifier is a preset (.awpreset), not an .awtheme.
Nothing else is allowed in the zip.

A theme is data: colours, numbers and pictures. The format has no place for a stylesheet, markup or a script, and the reader refuses any entry that is not one of the three above. An imported theme therefore has nothing it could run, no URL it could fetch and no way to reach the network. AW Next builds the stylesheet itself from the values in theme.json, as for any theme you edit in Settings. For the same reason a user stylesheet theme cannot be exported. A .css in %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next\themes still works and appears in the picker, but Export refuses it. Share the .css itself instead.

Field Meaning --- --- format Always aw-theme. Anything else is not a theme package. formatVersion The layout version. A reader refuses a higher number outright instead of guessing. name The name the theme installs under and the file is offered as: the editor name for a Custom theme, the name it travelled with for an imported one. Sanitised like a preset name, so one string works as all three. description, author, version, tags What the theme says about itself. All optional, all clamped. createdAt When it was exported, ISO 8601. app.createdWith The AW Next version that wrote it. Descriptive only. app.minVersion The oldest AW Next that can use it, as semver, or empty for any build that understands this format version. An older app refuses the import and says which version it needs. base Which built-in palette it started from, or empty. Descriptive only. assets The images the package carrie

The same nine-layer model the Custom theme editor writes: The five surface layers (bg, header, panel, card, settings) may carry an image, a fit (cover, contain, repeat, fill) and an effect (a coloured veil or a blur). The other four layers (text, muted, border, accent) are colours only. A colour is #rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa or rgb()/rgba(). The alpha half is the editor's opacity slider. image is the bare name of a file in assets/, never a path. A value with a separator, or naming a file the package does not carry, is refused. effect.blurImage is always empty in a package. The importing machine generates that copy from the source image and the effect settings, both of which travel. Everything that draws a theme makes those copies through app/util/themeBlur.js: the editor, an import, the preview shown before you apply one, and the picture the gallery publishes. sections.h: The picture a theme is judged by
sections.x: The preview in Settings before an import and the card in the theme gallery draw the same fixed sample of the application with the theme applied, built by app/util/themeMock.js from the sanitized theme model and nothing else. It shows the title bar, profile row, library, recently-unlocked list and settings surface, so every layer appears at least once. The sample is identical on any machine, at the same size. The gallery can therefore cache a rendered picture by the checksum of its file, and the Settings preview and a gallery card are the same image at different scales. The window sits on a fixed scene (a few CSS gradients in that file; no artwork, no network), because a see-through theme over nothing would read as a washed-out design. The sample text is a constant, so a picture never carries a library, account, path or game from the machine that drew it.

Nothing about the machine that exported the theme: Paths. An image is stored under a name built from its layer (bg.jpg, card-2.png), never its name on disk, because a wallpaper path can carry an account name, a game name or a private folder. Generated files. Blur and veil copies are rebuilt on the importing machine. Credit you did not type. author is empty unless the theme carries one, and an imported theme keeps its credit through a re-export.

Refused before anything is written, by the same reader in the app, in the gallery tooling and on the gallery server. --- --- Package 64 MB Any one file inside 24 MB Everything unpacked 48 MB Entries in the zip 32 Images 10 Expansion ratio 200x, so a zip built to be unpacked rather than read is refused Image size 12000 px per side, 40 megapixels Image types PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, checked from the bytes, not the extension SVG is not allowed: it is a document with its own script and external-reference surface, and a theme layer only needs a picture. The gallery is stricter, because a file served to everybody from a page is not one somebody chose to open: 8 MB per package there.

In order; the first failure stops everything: The file exists, is a file, is not empty, and is under the package limit. It parses as a zip with no more entries than the limit. Every entry name is manifest.json, theme.json, or a single flat name under assets/. A name that does not clean up to exactly what the archive claimed is treated as a traversal attempt. The declared sizes stay under the per-file and total limits, and the archive does not claim to unpack to hundreds of times its own weight. manifest.json parses, says aw-theme, has a format version this build understands, has a usable name, and (if it states one) a minVersion this build satisfies. Every asset's real type and size are read from its own bytes, and the size that came out of the archive is checked against the limit again: the header can lie, the data cannot. theme.json parses and is re-clamped, with every image field chec

An imported theme is selected as pack:<name> in cfg/options.ini and drawn by the same generator as the Custom theme, so the window, the in-game overlay and the picker all see one shape and it behaves like a built-in. Deleting it removes the whole folder, generated copies included.

formatVersion is one integer, bumped only when a package written today would be misread by an older build. Adding a field an older reader ignores does not count; changing what an existing field means does. A reader refuses a higher formatVersion, saying a newer AW Next made the file. A reader accepts every lower version it has supported. Fields added since are absent and take their defaults. app.minVersion covers behaviour, not layout: a theme that needs a layer or effect from a given release states it there, and an older app refuses the import and names the version. Current version: 1.

Anything a user reads on screen. There are three routes into the locale files: Markup with a stable id or list position. app/view/app.html carries English text as the reference copy and app/locale/loader.js overwrites it for the selected language. A new row needs its binding in the loader in the same change. t('slug', 'English', 'Français') for strings built in JavaScript: dialogs, menus, busy labels. The slug resolves to dialogs.<slug> in the locale files, which are the source of truth. The two literals are a safety net for a catastrophic locale failure, not a translation. localeText('dotted.path') for a label that already exists elsewhere in the locale tree. It returns an empty string when the locale has not loaded, because a blank label is a visible bug and a silently English one is not. The standalone Watchdog process cannot read the renderer locale files, so its few strings are mirr

Logs and diagnostics. parser.log and notification.log are read by the maintainer and pasted into issues; a log in twenty-eight languages is a log nobody can search. Thrown Error messages. The dialog around an error is localized and the message is shown as technical detail. Half a sentence in the reader's language and half in English is worse than either. File names, registry paths, INI keys, protocol values, source identifiers. steam, epic-official, steamsettings, %APPDATA%\Achievement Watcher Next are addresses, not words. Product and format names. "Steam / GBE Fork", "Ubisoft / Uplay R1/R2", "Goldberg". Dates, relative times, durations, numbers and percentages. See below.

sections.h: Dates, numbers and durations come from Intl
sections.x: app/util/intlFormat.js is the only place that formats a value rather than a sentence. It maps the app's language id to a BCP-47 tag and hands the work to the platform: Value API --- --- A date or a timestamp Intl.DateTimeFormat "3 days ago", "yesterday" Intl.RelativeTimeFormat Played time Intl.DurationFormat Counts and percentages Intl.NumberFormat "Steam, GOG and Epic" Intl.ListFormat The locale files carry the sentence and Intl carries the value. The Game Health footer is the model: dialogs.gh-verified-when is "Achievements checked {when}" in every language, and {when} is what Intl.RelativeTimeFormat produces. That is one key per language instead of one each for today, yesterday and N days ago, each a chance to get a plural rule wrong. The sandboxed overlay window cannot read app/locale/steam.json, so the BCP-47 table is spelled out in intlFormat.js; test/core/intlFormat.test.js reconc

Every Achievement Watcher address the app can open lives in app/util/links.js: home, download, documentation, the individual documentation pages, presets, issues, security, the upstream credits. Nothing else may spell one out. Markup names the destination instead of the address: applyExternalLinks() in app/app.js fills the href in at startup. test/core/links.test.js checks that every documentation slug resolves to a page the site publishes, and tools/locale-lint.js fails the build if an address is written by hand anywhere else. A repository rename is then one edit.
The site has two parts, localized differently.

The guides are English only, by decision. They are the same Markdown files GitHub renders in the repository; the site adds a shared layout (docs/layouts/default.html) with the header, contents list and guide list, and leaves the Markdown alone. Twenty-eight forked copies would drift apart at different speeds, and a translation two releases behind serves a reader worse than current English. Each page declares its language (site.lang: the <html lang> attribute, content-language and a self hreflang, from docs/layouts/default.html and docs/includes/head-custom.html), which is what browser translation and screen readers read. The in-app Help tab is the localized documentation: translated into all 28 languages, tailored to the reader's configuration, and what the app points at first. Its links lead here for the long form. A maintained translation of the guides would go in a sibling directory w

sections.h: The home page and the two galleries
sections.x: These three are hand-written pages, translated one language at a time without forking anything. Nine languages are complete: French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese (Brazil), Polish, Russian, Japanese and Simplified Chinese, all languages the application is already translated into. English lives in the markup: every visible string is in docs/index.html, docs/gallery/index.html and docs/gallery/themes/index.html and carries data-i18n, so the pages are complete and indexable before a script runs. That covers the navigation, both galleries, the submission forms and everything their scripts say back to a sender, validation refusals included. A translation is an overlay: a flat JSON file of key to string in docs/assets/i18n/, applied over that markup after load. A missing key falls back to the English on the page. --- --- Start a language node tools/site/extract-strings.js > docs/assets/

Add the key to app/locale/lang/english.json, the structural reference. Add a real translation to the other 27 files. The loader would show the English text for a missing or empty key, but the parity tests fail on one, so a gap never ships. A t() slug belongs under dialogs. Keep the placeholder set identical to English. Markup with a position in a list needs its nth-child selector in app/locale/loader.js updated in the same change. Differential downloads are on. electron-builder publishes a .blockmap with each installer, and electron-updater fetches only the blocks that changed since the installed version instead of the full 127 MB. The base it patches is installer.exe in the update cache, which every install rewrites from the installer that just ran. The differential downloader checks the patched file, and a mismatch falls back to the full download. If that fails its checksum, the app clears the cache and retries once before offering the release page.

electron-updater keeps the last downloaded installer in pending\, beside the installer.exe base: 254 MB for one version. On the first check of each run the app removes pending\ once the version in it is installed. A newer download waiting there (held back while a game runs) stays.

Before installing, the app checks the installer's Authenticode signature (app/util/updateSignature.js, app/util/authenticode.js). The check runs inside the app and starts no other program: behaviour engines such as Bitdefender's block a PowerShell process doing it. It refuses: an unsigned installer; an installer signed by anyone but CN=Shirow; a CN=Shirow installer whose certificate thumbprint is not pinned; a file modified after it was signed; a signature that does not verify against the pinned key. The certificate block of any release is public, so the app verifies each signature layer against its certificate and recomputes the PE hash it covers instead of trusting a block that only names the signer.
